Subject Nathan Rabin.
Made by D. S. I. Logan. Forwarded by D. I. Crawford.

Information has been received from a reliable source to the effect that Nathan Rabin, who recently returned from North China where he is stated to have married a Russian girl from Harbin, has been seen during the last few days loitering on Avenue Edward VII, in the vicinity of the China Press Building and Evening Post & Mercury Building.

According to information from the same source, Rabin was in the Paramount Ballroom, Yu Yuen Road, on the night of 25.7.40, where he was overheard to state that Harry Stuckold, Publisher of the Chinese American Daily News (pro-Chungking) will be killed within the next six weeks. (Note : Stuckold is believed to be returning to U.S.A. about the middle of September, 1940. Rabin was also overheard remarking that no distinction will be made between foreigners and Chinese and that if the foreign newspapermen who are on the Wang Ching Wei black list fail to leave China they will meet the same fate as their Chinese colleagues.

Rabin was observed to write his name, address and telephone No., on a piece of paper and pass it to one of his companions, as follows :-

Sir,

Further communication received by Mr. Gordon
Campbell, U. S. Marshall for China, from the Immigration and
Naturalization Service of the U. S. Dept. of Labour, definitely
show that Rabin's claim to American citizenship is entirely
without foundation.

Immigration records show that Nathan Rabin alias
Rabinovitch was born in Kopul, Russia, on September 12th, 1909,
and that his father Mendel Rabinovitch was born in Dvinsk,
Latvia, formerly Russia. Rabinovitch resided in the U.S.A.
from April 1928 until his deportation on November 4th, 1932.

Rabin's antecedents were traced by Immigration
officials through his maternal aunt, Mrs. Eva Goorwitch,
residing Apartment No. 302, No. 1761 Seward Avenue, Detroit,
Michigan, U.S.A. Dr. Bella Rabinovitch, a sister of Rabin's
on being contacted, made a sworn statement to Immigration
officials, giving the aforementioned particulars of her
brother's antecedents. He left Seattle, Washington, U.S.A.,
per S.S. "Princess Alice" for Shanghai on November 14th, 1932.
He was accompanied by his aunt and uncle Eva, and Boris
Goorwitch, who apparently, subsequently returned to the U.S.A.,
and are now residing at the aforementioned address in Detroit.

Made by and Forwarded by D. I. Glover

Sir,

During the morning of the 3rd May 1939,
D.S.I. Crighton and the undersigned interviewed Mr.
Gordon Campbell, Marshall of the U. S. Court for China,
who has been making enquiries with reference to Nathan
Rabin's claim to American citizenship.

Mr. Campbell handed over copies of radiograms
which he had received from the U. S. Department of
Labour, Washington, a Federal Agent in Detroit,
Michigan, and a resume of the results of his own
personal investigations made locally.

The result of these enquiries show that Rabin,
whose real name is Nathan Rabinovitch, is actually a
Russian Jew, who was born at Kopul or Kowul in Russia,
although he at one time claimed that he was born in
Latvia. He entered the U.S.A. in 1928 under non-quota
visae No. 50, issued at Harbin on the 29th February
1928, which entitled him to remain in that country for
a period of six months. For some unaccountable reason
the Immigration Officials lost trace of him, and he
remained in America until he was deported on the 4th
November 1932. Whilst in the U.S.A. he resided in
Detroit, Michigan, his last known address being No. 341
Leicester Court in that city, where his parents then
resided. He appears to have been employed between July
1928 and February 1929 as a motor-car salesman by Messrs.
Lawrence Motor Sales Coy., of Detroit, whilst between
September 1928 and February 1931 he attended Detroit

He was later employed in the same capacity at Ciro's

On the 20th, March 1939, it was learned that
Rabin, alias Rakens, alias Raven, had on the 6th
March 1939 endeavoured to persuade Mr. Ralph Lynn
(British), proprietor of a dancing studio at No. 191
Hart Road to permit one of his rooms to be used by
some Chinese, and Japanese, who desired that their
meeting should be private. Lynn consented, and at the
appointed time, Rabin arrived accompanied by three
Japanese. The four of them went to Lynn's living
room where they remained for about two hours. As
no Chinese arrived to keep the appointment, Lynn who
was conducting dancing classes at the time, became
suspicious and went to investigate. He was just in
time to see Rabin, and the three Japanese, leaving
the premises with drawn pistols in their hands. They
entered a large limousine, but Lynn, being somewhat
flustered, failed to note the number of the car.

Enquiries have been made at H.B.M.'s Passport
Office regarding George Hoshinoya alleged to be in
possession of a Canadian passport, but no record
of this individual could be found.

Since forwarding the last report no further
information has been obtained about Rabin, who
apparently fearing reprisals for his part in bringing

prefers to remain in Japanese occupied territory.

Sir,

The attached memo reveals an attempt
by Nathan Rabin to hurl some unknown Chinese to Mr .
Ralph Lynn's Dancing Studio at 191 Hart Road on
the night of March 6, 1939. The fact that Rabin
was accompanied on that occasion by three Japanese
is sufficient to indicate that he was acting as an
agent provocateur for the Japanese Special Service
Section. The memo was obtained from the U.S.
Consul General with whose permission I forward it
for information.

D.S.I. Rhind

(COPY)

Shanghai, March 16, 1939.

The matter is presumed to be of interest to the U.S.
authorities, apart from its general political significance,
because it involves one Nathan Rakens (Nathan Rabin) who claims
U.S. citizenship and to have a U.S. passport. Rakens has been
around Shanghai for some years, has an unsavory reputation, and
at one time for a short while was nominal manager of The Little
Club on Bubbling Well Road.

On March 6 Rakens, who has an extensive acquaintance
among the "night-life" world of Shanghai, asked Ralph Lynn if
he could use one of the rooms at Lynn's studio for a meeting,
so he told Lynn, between some Chinese and Japanese who desired
that their meeting should be private. Rakens told Lynn that
the meeting would not last more than five minutes. Lynn
consented and at the time fixed Rakens arrived accompanied by
three Japanese and the four of them went to Lynn's living room.
At the time Lynn was conducting classes in the studio. He
noticed that Rakens seemed nervous and went out two or three
times, evidently looking for the Chinese who were expected. Two
hours passed but no Chinese arrived. Lynn, becoming suspicious
decided to investigate, and saw Rakens and the three Japanese
leaving the house, all with pistols in their hands; they went
away in a large limousine motor car but Lynn, being flustered,
failed to note its license number.

Lynn was advised not to mention the incident to anyone
until the U.S. authorities had time to investigate the matter,
and Lynn said he would not. Lynn formed the opinion that
Rakens and the Japanese had planned to lure some Chinese to
Lynn's apartment and perhaps kill him there, but the Chinese
did not come. Lynn can be found at the above address. He
probably knows where Rakens lives or can be found.

RESUME OF INVESTIGATIONS MADE CONCERNING
THE ACTIVITIES OF ONE, NATHAN RABIN.

On February 26, 1939, information was received
to the effect that a British subject, named H. H. GOFF,
was endeavouring to sell illegally one hundred "MAUSER"
automatic pistols and ammunition. Enquiries revealed
that Goff is in partnership with one, named "BRAN" or
"BRAND" in the Native Industry Co., Room No. 503, No.169
Yuen Ming Yuen Road, Tel. No. 10751.

On March 1, 1939, a foreigner called at Police
Headquarters and stated that a man, named N. RABIN, alias
RAVEN, who resided at No. 33, Lane No. 150, Tifeng Road,
(Tel. No. 23163) and was alleged to be employed by the
Japanese Secret Service, had commissioned him to find a
buyer for the undermentioned arms and ammunition :-

1 ) 10 machine guns, 50.c.m. in length, weight
12 lbs. each, firing 500 rounds per
minute, complete with magazine and
20,000 rounds per gun @ $2,500.oo each.
Total $ 25,000.oo.

2.) 50 Full Mauser Auto Pistols (1936 model),
each complete with one magazine (20 shots)
and 250 rounds of ammunition each, @
$260.oo each.
Total $ 13.000.oo.

Rabin first proposed that he should interest
himself in this deal when they met outside the Navy Y.M.C.A.

- 2 -

on February 25, 1939. During the conversation
he mentioned to the informer that if he succeeded
in finding a buyer, he could communicate with him
(Rabin) either through Bran (Brand ?) at the Native
Industry Co. Yuen Ming Yuen Road or through a
Japanese known as "GEORGE" (Tel. No. 41346), whom
the informer knew to be a member of the Japanese
Secret Service.

Telephone No. 41346 is listed under the
name of "Y. KUWAHATA, Lane No. 24, House No. 18, North
Haining Road."

. Subsequent meetings took place between
the informer and Rabin at the Navy Y.M.C.A. and
later he (informer) met Bran (?) in his office at
No. 169 Yuen Ming Yuen Road.

On one occasion during Bran's temporary
absence from the office, Goff who works together
with Bran, warned the informer to be careful of
Rabin. Asked if he thought it was a bogus deal,
Goff stated that he had nothing whatever to do with
it and could not say whether it was genuine or not,
but he was very suspicious of Rabin. He was,
however, able to state that Bran (?) had assured
him that he had some of the guns which were being
offered for sale.

Enquiries made by detectives show that the
telephone number (23163) given by Rabin as his private

- 3 -

number, is listed under the name of "SANDY GUTTERMAN",
House No. 33, Lane No. 15C, Tifeng Road. Gutterman
incidentally is at present in the Phillipine Islands,
having left Shanghai after being involved in a
fraudulent narcotic deal.

From enquiries made at the U.S. Consulate
General, it was learned that Rabin's claim to American
citizenship is without foundation.

Acting upon the information obtained, the
police arranged for the informer to introduce a
Chinese detective to Rabin as a prospective buyer
at a meeting which was to take place at the Chocolate
Shop, Nanking Road. Consequently, at 9.45 a.m. on
March 2nd. 1939, the introduction was made. The
detective, who assumed the role of "middleman",
discussed the conditions to purchase the second
described consignment of arms, consisting of "Mauser"
pistols. Rabin then stated that the pistols did
not actually belong to him, and that he was only
acting for the owner who resided in the French
Concession. He stipulated that the purchase money
should be delivered to an address in the French
Concession, to which he would lead the detective, and
where if everything was satisfactory, the arms would be
delivered. The detective objected to this arrangement
and proposed the International Settlement, claiming
that it would be much safer for him under this condition.

- 4 -

This terminated the interview, but it was agreed to
meet the following morning at the same place. At
the time appointed, the informer and the Chinese
detective met Rabin. The latter stated that the
seller had agreed to the stipulation made by the
purchaser to the effect that the sale should be
effected in the International Settlement. The seller,
however, stipulated that the money, $13,000.00 in
notes, should be produced for inspection prior to the
delivery of the arms. The detective protested that
this would leave the buyer open to either being held
up and robbed or defrauded by some other means. Rabin
then stated that he would have to leave the matter in
abeyance until he had consulted the owner on this point.
A further meeting was arranged for 5:45 p.m.
the same day. The parties met at the Chocolate Shop
as arranged, and on this occasion, Rabin suggested that
in order to allay the detective's suspicion, he should
provide himself with bodyguards. They should proceed
by motor car to an address to which he would lead them.
On arrival, the owner of the pistols would inspect the
money whilst they were in the car. They would then
proceed to inspect the pistols, after which the transfer
would be effected. This concluded the meeting, but
they arranged to meet again at 10:15 a.m. on the 4th.
March 1939.
At the appointed time, they again met, when

- 5 -

Rabin was informed by the detective that the suggestion
made the previous day was unacceptable to the buyer.
The detective stipulated that the arms be delivered to
a place to be designated by him, but this was refused.
A further meeting took place at 5:30 p.m.
March 4th. 1939, but as no satisfactory arrangement
could be arrived at, no further meetings were arranged.
At 8:45 p.m. 6.3.39, C.P.C.2018 on traffic
duty at the intersection of Avenue and Seymour Roads,
who was accompanied by a Mr. S.Abolnik, residing at
Apt. "C" 2, No.1248 Rue Lafayette, French Concession,
went to Bubbling Well Police Station, where they made
the following report :-
At about 8.35 p.m. 6.3.39 an unidentified
motor car was proceeding on Avenue Road from West to
East with another motor car of the "Nash" or "Buick"
type, S.M.C. No.5601, following behind. When about
five yards west of Seymour Road, motor car No.5601
stopped quickly with a screech of brakes. Immediately
following this, a man was heard to cry out, as if in
pain. Four Japanese in civilian clothing were then
seen to jump from the car, pick up a male Chinese from
the roadway and bundle him into the car. C.P.C.2018
observed that the Chinese was bleeding profusely from
the head, whilst Mr. Abolnik noticed that he was wearing
some sort of dark coloured long gown. The car was
stationary only a very short period, a matter of seconds,
before it was driven away in an easterly direction.
Neither the C.P.C. nor Mr. Abolnik saw pistols or other

- 6 -

weapons.
On checking the registration of
private motor car No. 5601, it was found to be in
the name of "YOSHINOBU KUWAHATA" (Japanese) who
resides at Lane 24, House 18, Haining Road.
Detectives attached to Bubbling Well
Station made enquiries and requested the assistance
of the Japanese Consular Police to visit the home
of the registered owner of the car in question.
Sgt. Matsumoto of the Japanese Consular
Police, however, refused to give the required assistance,
stating that his department would fully investigate the case
and forward the result of same to the Police in
due course.
At 4.00 p.m. 7.3.39 D.S. Nagamune, attached to
Bubuling Well, interviewed Sgt. Matsumoto at the
Japanese Consulate and learned that S.M.C. Licence
Plates No. 5601 were attached to a two-seater
Citroen coupe parked in Lane No. 24, Haining Road,
which had not been used since January, 1939.
Examination of the car at 5 p.m. 7.3.39
by D.S. Nagamune showed that the car had not been
used for some considerable period, the tyres were
flat, the inside floorboards were missing and the
upholstery was covered with a thick layer of dirt.
At 9.30 a.m. 8.3.39 the car was
re-inspected by D.S. Ware, attached to Bubbling Well
Station, who found that the report made by D.S. Nagamune

- 7 -

as to the condition of same was correct.
Enquiries made at the Traffic Office
elicited the information that licence plates No.
5601 were issued on the 26.7.38 to "YOSHINOBU
KAWAHATA" in respect of his "Opel" motor car, which
is a 12 h.p. four cylinder, four seater open touring
car, engine No. M. 835164. The predominant colour
is green with green disc wheels and a luggage carrier
fitted. The application was renewed on the 8.2.39.
A search of the files showed that a Japanese
named "GEORGE HOSHINOYA", residing House No. 18,
Lane no. 24, Haining Road , was passed as a capable
driver by the S.M.P. on the 28.9.38. The car used
by Hoshinoya was an "Opel" car, Lic. No. 5601. This
man is apparently the "Mr. George" whom Rabin referred
to.
At 11 a.m. March 11th. 1939, Mr. O. Boisseree
(British), Coal Merchant, residing Flat No. 3, 1033
Bubbling Well Road, trading as the U.S. Oriental Trading
Co. No. 133 Yuen Ming Yuen Road, called at Bubbling
Well Station, where he made the following report :-
On March 3rd. 1939, a Mr. Wong Tseu Wei
(王祖惠.), aged 40 years, native of Canton, broker,
residing at No. 37 Sun Avenue, asked him if at a later
date, he would act as a witness concerning a business
deal he intended to transact. Wong produced a document
in Chinese, which he claimed, authorised him to act on

- 8 -

behalf of the Chinese Government.

Mr. Boisseree stated that as he had
known Wong for some time, he agreed to oblige him.
He was asked to meet Wong outside the "Weida" Hotel,
993 Avenue Joffre, French Concession, at 6 p.m.
March 6th, 1939. They met at the appointed time
and place and proceeded to a room in the hotel,
where Mr. Boisseree saw a sum of approximately
$5,000.00 on a table. There were about seven
male Chinese in the room at the time, and a foreigner
present, whom Mr. Boisseree had seen on several
occasions. The meeting broke up at about 6.30 p.m.
and the money was taken away by Wong and another male
Chinese, whereupon all left the hotel. Mr. Boisseree
claimed that he was unaware of the nature of the
transaction, although he suspected that it concerned
an arms deal.

On leaving the hotel, Mr. Boisseree parted
company with Wong, but before doing so, noticed that

foreigner in a motor car lic. No. 5601, which was parked
outside.

foreigner, with whom Wong was last seen, was Nathan Rabin,
who formerly resided at No. 33 Tifeng Road.

From enquiries made at Wong's residence,
No. 37 Sun Avenue, it was found that this person was
employed as an accountant, at a salary of $100.00 per
month, at the Metropole Garden Cabaret, Gordon Road.

- 9 -

His wife who stated that she had not seen her
husband since the evening of the 6th. March, 1939,
claimed complete ignorance as to his business matters.
At 9 a.m. March 13th. 1939, the informer
called on Rabin at Apt. No. 611, Broadway Mansions,
to which he had removed, following the abduction of
Wong. The informer noted on glancing at a date
block, lying on a desk, that Rabin had noted an
appointment for 10 a.m. that morning with Colonel
Agaki, Chief of the Intelligence Service. He also
noticed that an auto. pistol was lying in a half
opened drawer. During the ensuing conversation,
the informer told Rabin that the "buyer" for the
"Mauser" pistols insisted that the guns be delivered
to an address which he would designate, and that he
on no account would agree to any other proposal as
to accompanying Rabin or any other individual to
unknown addresses. Rabin then suggested that the
"buyer" should meet him that evening in the lounge
of the "Cathay" Hotel, where they could talk over
the proposed transaction. This proposition was,
however, later vetoed on the grounds that it would
be unwise to jeopardise the safety of the Chinese
detective, who was acting as the "buyer", as by this
time, it was very apparent that Rabin was acting in
the capacity of "agent provocation" for the Japanese
Secret Service.
The name of RUDOLPH W. MAYER (American)
who trades under the name of the Far Eastern Syndicate,

- 10 -

Room No.2C5, Hamilton House, has been mentioned
as an associate of Rabin, but so far no information
has been obtained to connect him with activities
on behalf of the Japanese Authorities.

On the 16th. March, 1939, a prisoner
named TSEU YAH VUNG (周統文), arrested in
connection with C.l Misc. 29/39, who had recently
been returned by the Japanese Gendarmerie after
having been in their custody for three days, had
made the following statement : -

He stated that whilst he was in the
custody of the Japanese Gendarmerie at Bridge House,
he got into conversation with a Cantonese prisoner,
named Wong, who stated that he had been arrested
with one other, whilst negotiating an arms deal with
a foreigner. They had first visited the "Weida"
Hotel and had then been driven by the foreigner to
Hart Road, where a number of Japanese surrounded the
car and arrested them.

He subsequently learned in a conversation
he had with another prisoner, named YOONG CHIEN TOONG
(熊劍東), that they had been arrested together
and that Wong was supposed to be an employee of the
Metropole Ball Room.

Yoong Chien Toeng was formerly the leader
of a Chinese Guerilla Unit, which operated in the
Shanghai Area. A number of his followers were arrested
during January, 1938, subsequently handed over to the

- 11 -

On the 20th. March, 1939, it was learned

to pursuade Mr. RALPH LYNN ( British ), Proprietor

one of his rooms to be used by some Chinese and
Japanese, who desired that their meeting should be
private. Lynn, consented and at the appointed time,
Rabin arrived accompanied by three Japanese. The
four of them went to Lynn's living room, where they
remained for about two hours. As no Chinese arrived

dancing classes at the time, became suspicious and
went to investigate. He was just in time to see Rabin
and the three Japanese leaving the premises with drawn
pistols in their hands. They entered a large
limousine, but Lynn, being somewhat flustered, failed
to note the number of the car.

On nearing the Veida Hotel, Rabin suggested

Entering the room, they met a number of

As soon as the door was unlocked, Mr. Read

Rabin came out with two of the Chinese and

Mr. Read then spoke to Mr. Boisserie and

- 4 -

the "East Asia Trading Coy.", General Merchants &
Commission Agents, No. 131 Museum Road (Tele. No. 18366),
was introduced to the D. C. (Special Branch) as a person
who wished to divulge certain information regarding the
illegal sale of arms. Mr. Jellinek, who resides at
Room No. 8, No. 121 Wayside Road (Tele. No. 50929),
served as a member of the S.M.P. (Specials) during the
recent hostilities. On being referred to C.S.I. Smith,
he stated that a certain man, who claimed American
citizenship, named H. Rubin/alias Raven, who resided at
No. 33, Lane No. 150, Tifeng Road (Tele. No. 25183) and
was alleged to be employed by the Japanese secret
service, had commissioned him to find a buyer for the
undermentioned arms and ammunition :-

1. Ten machine guns, 30 c.m. in length, weight
12 lbs. each, firing 500 rounds per minute,
complete with magazines and 20,000 rounds

- 4 -

per gun @ $2,500.00 each.
Total : $25,000.00.

2. 50 Full auto: Mauser pistols (1936 Model)
each complete with one magazine (20 shots)
and 250 rounds of ammunition each,
@ $260.00 each.
Total : $13,000.00.

Rabin first proposed that he should interest
himself in this deal when they met outside the Navy
Y.M.C.A. on the 25th February 1939. During the
conversation he mentioned that if Mr. Jellinek
succeeded in finding a buyer he could communicate with
him, either through Brun (Brand ?) at Room No. 303,
No. 169 Yuen Ming Yuen Road, or through a Japanese
known as "George" (Tele. No. 41346). Mr. Jellinek
recollected that he had met "George" previously, and
that he was a member of the Japanese Secret Service.

It was ascertained from enquiries made that
Tele. No. 41346 is listed under the name of Y. Kawabata,
of Lane No. 84, House No. 18, North Haining Road.

Subsequent meeting took place between Mr.
Jellinek and Rabin at the Navy Y.M.C.A. and later he met
Brun (?) in his office at No. 169 Yuen Ming Yuen Road.

On one occasion during Brun's temporary
absence from the office, Goff who works together with

- 5 -

this man, warned Mr. Jellinek to be careful of Rabin.
Asked if he thought that it was a bogus deal, Goff
stated that he had nothing to do with it whatsoever,
and could not say whether it was genuine or not, but
he was very suspicious of Rabin. He was, however,
able to state that Bran (?) had assured him that he had
seen some of the guns which were being offered for sale.

From enquiries made at the U. S. Consulate
General by C.D.I. Grubb it was ascertained that Rabin
is not an American citizen.

Further enquiries elicited that Tele. No.
23163 given by Rabin as his private telephone number,
is listed under the name of Sandy Gutterman, of House
No. 33, Lane No. 180, Tifeng Road. Whether this person
is one named Alex Leo Gutterman (Z.943 & C.47/35) who
has a previous conviction cannot at the present be
ascertained.

Following the receipt of this information
it was arranged that Mr. Jellinek should introduce Det.
Inspr. Chm Shou Ling, attached to this branch, to Rabin
as a prospective buyer at a meeting which he would
arrange for the following day at the "Chocolate Shop",
Nanking Road.

At 9.45 a.m. March 2nd, 1939, Mr. Jellinek
introduced D.I. Chm to Rabin. D.I. Chm, representing

- 6 -

himself as a "middleman", discussed the conditions to
purchase the second described consignment of arms,
consisting of Mauser pistols. Rabin then stated that
the pistols did not actually belong to him, and that
he was only acting as a broker for the owner, who
resided in the French Concession. He stipulated that
the purchase money should be delivered by D.I. Chu to
an address in the French Concession, to which he would
lead him, and where if everything was satisfactory the
arms would be delivered. D.I. Chu objected to the deal
being consummated in the French Concession, and proposed
the International Settlement, claiming that it would be
much safer for him under this condition. This
terminated the interview, but it was agreed to meet the
following morning at the same place. At the time
appointed Mr. Jellinek and D.I. Chu again met Rabin.
The latter stated that the seller had agreed to the
stipulation made by the purchaser to the effect that
the sale should be effected in the International
Settlement. The seller, however, stipulated that the
money, $12,000.00 in notes, should be produced for
inspection prior to the delivery of the arms. This,
D.I. Chu protested, would leave the buyer open to either
being held up and robbed or by some other means

- 7 -

defrauded. Rabin then stated that he would have to
leave the matter in abeyance until he had consulted
the owner on this point. The interview was then
concluded, but it was arranged that a further meeting
should take place at the same place that afternoon at
5.45 p.m.

At 4 p.m. the same day, Mr. Jellinek called
on C.D.I. Grubb, and during the ensuing conversation
mentioned that Rabin had been associated with Rudolph
Mayer (American), but that he was, as far as he knew,
not connected with this alleged arms deal.

At 5.45 p.m. D.I. Gin and Mr. Jellinek met
Rabin at the "Chocolate Shop". On this occasion Rabin
suggested that in order to allay D.I. Gin's suspicions,
that he should provide himself with bodyguards. They
should proceed by motorcar to an address, to which he
would lead them. On arrival the owner of the pistols
would inspect the money whilst they were in the car.
They would then proceed to inspect the pistols, after
which the transfer would be effected. This concluded
the meeting, but they arranged to meet again at 10.35
a.m. on the 4th March 1936. At the appointed time, they
again met, when Rabin was informed by D.I. Gin that the
suggestion made the previous day was unacceptable to the

- 8 -

buyer. D.I. Chu stipulated that the arms be delivered
to a place to be designated by him, but this was
refused. A further meeting took place at 5.30 p.m.
March 4th, 1939, but as no satisfactory arrangement
could be arrived at no further meetings were arranged.
According to Mr. Jellinek, Rabin is still
anxious to proceed with the business, and as soon as
he makes any further suggestions he will communicate
with the undersigned.
Whether or not Rabin is trying to negotiate
a genuine arms deal cannot at the moment be ascertained,
but if he is not, he is either planning to defraud any
prospective buyer, or is merely in the employ of the
Japanese Secret Service as an Agent Provocateur in
arresting leaders of Guerilla Units who might want to
purchase arms for their various units engaged in anti-
Japanese activities.
In a conversation with D.S.I. Rhind,
Officer 1/c **〔此处转录不清〕**, the undersigned learned that
Rabin is at the moment living at the Nifong Road
address with George Leonoff (Russian), whilst Sandy
Guttmann, who is listed as the subscriber to the
telephone at that address, is at present in the
Philippine Island, where he fled after having been

- 9 -

concerned in a shady deal concerning narcotics. D.S.I.
Rhind was also able to inform the undersigned that
Kuwahata, who at the moment is also absent from
Shanghai, is a notorious narcotic trafficker, and some
time ago was concerned in selling drugs to Italian
Officers of the M.V. "Conte Biancamano".

On being shown a photograph of Rubin by
Chief Inspr. Hall of the Traffic Dept., the undersigned
recognised him as a man known as Nathan, who at one time
conducted an Orchestra at Ciro's and the Little Club.
This man is a low type of Jew, wholly unscrupulous and
just the person to commit a particularly mean type of
fraud. In view of this, it would appear that the whole
thing is nothing more than an attempted fraud or
possibly he is being employed by the Japanese to locate
leaders of Guerilla troops.

During the afternoon of the 8th March 1938,
Mr. Jellinek informed C.D.I. Crubb and the undersigned
that he had received a telephone message from Rubin
asking him to call at House No. 18, Lane 24, North
Haining Road. As Mr. Jellinek knew that this address
was being used by the Japanese Secret Service, he asked
if it was advisable for him to go or not. C.D.I. Crubb
and the undersigned advised him not to go, but to ring
up this address and ask Rubin to meet him on Nanking Road.

- 10 -

He did as he was instructed and was told by "George"
that Rabin was not there.

Mr. Jellinek was able to inform the under-
signed that "George" was a well educated Japanese, who
appeared to hold a high position in the Japanese Secret
Service, as he frequently travelled between Shanghai
and Tokyo by plane.

Later in the day, Mr. Jellinek informed the
undersigned that following the receipt of a further
telephone message, he had met Rabin outside House No.
18, Lane No. 24, North Haining Road. Rabin stated
that he had learned from a friend in the U. S. Consulate
that the Police were making enquiries about him, and
in consequence he had removed to North Haining Road
until the matter had blown over. Mr. Jellinek assured
him that he knew nothing of the matter, and Rabin then
stated that he suspected that Goff had given information
to the Police.

Efforts are now being made to ascertain more
details regarding the activities of Rabin, which will be
reported on at a later date.

M. C. Flower
D. I.

Abduction of a male Chinese by Japanese
in civilian clothing.

At 8.45 p.m. 6-3-39 C.P.C. 2018 (traffic duty
at the intersection of Avenue and Seymour Roads)
and Mr. S. Abolnik who resides at Apt. C.2, No.1248
Rue Lafayette, came to Bubbling Well Station and
made the following report:-

At about 8.35 p.m. 6-3-39 an unidentified m/car
was proceeding on Avenue Road from west to east with
another m/car of the "Nash" or "Buick" type S.M.C.
No.5601, following behind. When about five yards west
of Seymour Road m/car S.M.C. No.5601 stopped quickly
with the brakes screeching. Immediately following
this a Chinese was heard to cry out in pain as, or
after four Japanese in civilian clothes dismounted from
the car, picked up a male Chinese from the roadway
and bundled him into the car. C.P.C. 2018 observed
that the Chinese was bleeding profusely from the
head, and Mr. Abolnik noticed that he was wearing
some sort of dark long gown. The car was stationary
only a very short period, a matter of seconds, before
it was driven away eastward.

Neither C.P.C. 2018 nor Mr. Abolnik saw pistols
or other weapons .

Misc. No. 11L/39

1 (Sheet 2)

The intersection where this occurrence happened
is purely residential, there being no shops or alleys
where additional witnesses might be found for many yards.

On checking the registration of private m/car 5601,
it was found to be in the name of Yoshinobu Kuwahata
who lives at **〔此处转录不清〕** 24, House 18 Maining Road.

D.S. Magamure and the undersigned proceeded to
Hongkew Station and learned that no report of the
occurrence been made there (should it have been a
peculiar accident).

The same detectives then proceeded to the offices
of the Japanese Consular Police for assistance to visit
the home of Yoshinobu Kuwahata. Japanese Consular
Sgt. Matsumoto refused to give assistance and stated
that his department would fully investigate the case
and inform Bubbling Well Station of the result on
7-3-39.

No enquiries have been made by the public con-
cerning the missing Chinese and no hospital reports
have been received.

Should this occurrence be an abduction it must
have been carefully planned with the car waiting nearby
with the engine running; otherwise meeting the victim
in the middle of the road suggests a fortuitous
coincidence.

Misc. No. 130/39

1 (Sheet 3)

As an alternative to abduction, it is respectfully
suggested that it might be a hit-and-run accident in which
the car driver and occupants preferred to remove the
victim rather than be involved in police enquiries.
